```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "area_report_helpers.R"))
R <- readRDS(here::here("data", "value_added_review.rds"))   # R/21_value_added_review.R
A <- R$all; D <- R$disadvantaged

vs  <- function(x, s) x$variants$summary |> filter(spec == s)
imp <- function(x, lab) x$importance |> filter(label == lab)
om  <- function(x, v) x$omissions$r[x$omissions$var == v]
# (the coefficient table has a column called t, so the term argument is not)
cf  <- function(x, s, trm) x$variants$coefs |> filter(spec == s, term == trm)
pc  <- function(x, d = 0) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
# share of the local authority variance a variant accounts for
la_var <- function(x, s) 1 - (vs(x, s)$sd_la / vs(x, "published")$sd_la)^2
r2  <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
pe  <- function(b) sprintf("%+.1f%%", pct(b))         # a log-scale coefficient as a percentage
wn  <- function(x) x$design$within_vs_national
SPEC_LAB <- c(published = "Published", no_workforce = "– workforce", no_ofsted = "– Ofsted",
              intake_context = "– workforce – Ofsted", no_absence = "– absence",
              plus_l4 = "+ neighbourhood education", plus_route = "+ governance route",
              plus_mat = "+ trust membership", plus_sen = "+ SEN", plus_mobility = "+ mobility",
              plus_single_sex = "+ single-sex", plus_girls_pct = "+ share of girls",
              plus_size = "+ size", plus_religious = "+ religious character",
              candidate = "Candidate")
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Draft for discussion

A review of the value-added measure used across the
[How to Pull the Right Lever](https://adamdennett.github.io/school_attainment_tool/pulling_the_right_lever_v2.html)
work and the Sussex documents. Every figure comes from refitting the
published national model on its own data, `r format(R$n, big.mark = ",")`
school-years for `r format(R$n_schools, big.mark = ",")` schools,
2021/22 to 2024/25. Nothing uses pupil-level records.
:::

# Summary {.unnumbered}

**The measure is sound, and its core should stay as it is.** A
school-level residual from a multilevel model of Attainment 8 is the
right construction. The intake terms that do the work are the right
ones, and with four years of data a school's average value added is a
reliable signal (reliability `r r2(A$design$reliability_mean)` for all
pupils, `r r2(D$design$reliability_mean)` for disadvantaged pupils).

**But three things in the specification credit or penalise schools for
the wrong reasons, and fixing them would change the picture for a
meaningful minority of schools.**

1. **The Ofsted rating is in the expectation.** A school's expected
   result is set higher if Ofsted rated it highly, but Ofsted's
   judgement is partly based on those same results. Taking it out moves
   `r pc(vs(A, "no_ofsted")$moved_quintile)` of schools into a different
   value-added quintile.
2. **The workforce terms are things schools partly control.** They add
   little to the model, and teacher retention is the only one that moves
   schools noticeably (`r pc(imp(A, "Teacher retention")$moved_quintile)`
   change quintile without it). They are better treated as possible
   explanations of value added than as part of its baseline.
3. **Value added is measured within each local authority.** The
   expectation includes the authority's own effect, so a school in a
   strong authority is held to a higher bar. Measured against England
   instead, `r pc(wn(A)$moved_quintile[1])` of schools change quintile.

**Four additions are worth making**, all of them intake or context
rather than things a school controls:

- **pupil mobility**, the strongest new term (AIC
  `r round(vs(A, "plus_mobility")$delta_aic)`); value added at present
  penalises schools whose pupils arrive mid-phase;
- **a girls' school term**, since girls' schools currently gain
  `r pe(cf(A, "plus_single_sex", "single_sexGirls")$estimate)` from
  their intake's gender alone;
- **SEN support and EHCP rates**, which matter most for disadvantaged
  pupils;
- **neighbourhood education** (% with degree-level qualifications around
  the school), for all pupils. It removes value added's tilt towards
  schools in educated places and accounts for
  `r pc(la_var(A, "plus_l4"))` of the remaining local authority
  variance. Brighton and Hove's effect falls
  from `r ord(vs(A, "published")$bh_rank)` to
  `r ord(vs(A, "plus_l4")$bh_rank)` in England. It makes no difference
  for disadvantaged pupils.

**Governance (academy route, trust membership), school size and
religious character should stay out.** Who runs a school is part of
what value added should measure, not part of its baseline, and in any
case these terms barely move it.

Taken together the changes are substantial: the candidate measure
correlates `r r2(vs(A, "candidate")$r)` with the published one across
schools, and `r pc(vs(A, "candidate")$moved_quintile)` of schools
change quintile. Most of that is the Ofsted decision. The recommendations
are in @sec-recommendations.

# What the measure is

Value added is the residual of the published model, averaged over a
school's years:

$$\text{VA} = \text{Attainment 8} - \exp(\hat{y})\,e^{\sigma^2/2}$$

where $\hat{y}$ is the model's prediction of log Attainment 8 and the
second factor is the lognormal back-transformation. The model is

```
log(Attainment 8) ~ log(% FSM6) + log(absence) + log(% EAL) + KS2 (centred)
                    + admissions (selective) + segregation (LA)
                    + teacher retention + % teachers on leadership pay
                    + log(teacher sickness days)
                    + (1 | year) + (1 | Ofsted rating) + (1 | region / local authority)
```

fitted separately for all, disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils.
Two features of the prediction matter for what follows:

- **It includes every random effect**, so the expectation for a school
  already contains its Ofsted grade's effect and its local authority's
  effect. Value added is therefore "relative to schools with the same
  Ofsted grade in the same authority".
- **It is a residual, not a separately estimated school effect.** Each
  school-year's residual is averaged. @sec-signal checks that this is
  close to what a school random intercept would give.

# How much each term matters {#sec-importance}

Each term was dropped in turn. Two things were recorded: how much worse
the model fits (the rise in AIC, fitted by maximum likelihood), and how
much schools' value added moves.

```{r fig-importance}
#| fig-cap: "Each term of the published model dropped in turn. Left, the loss of fit (rise in AIC; bigger means the term matters more to the model). Right, the share of schools whose value added moves into a different quintile without it. All pupils and disadvantaged pupils."
#| fig-height: 6
bind_rows(A$importance |> mutate(group = "All pupils"),
          D$importance |> mutate(group = "Disadvantaged pupils")) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, rev(A$importance$label))) |>
  select(group, label, `Loss of fit (AIC)` = delta_aic, `Schools changing quintile (%)` = moved_quintile) |>
  mutate(`Schools changing quintile (%)` = 100 * `Schools changing quintile (%)`) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(group, label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, label, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`All pupils` = TEAL, `Disadvantaged pupils` = WARM), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Prior attainment and absence carry the model; the workforce terms barely register") +
  theme_note(10)
```

```{r tbl-importance}
#| tbl-cap: "The published model's terms, all pupils: standardised effect (the change in Attainment 8 for one standard deviation of the term, or the random effect's standard deviation), loss of fit without it, and how far school value added moves without it."
A$importance |>
  transmute(Term = label, `Standardised effect` = sprintf("%+.1f%%", std_effect_pct),
            `Loss of fit (AIC)` = round(delta_aic), `VA correlation without it` = sprintf("%.3f", r_va),
            `Mean VA change (points)` = sprintf("%.2f", mean_abs_change),
            `Schools changing quintile` = pc(moved_quintile)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrrr")
```

The ranking is clear:

- **Prior attainment and absence** are by far the most important terms.
  Each moves nearly half of schools a quintile when dropped.
- **The Ofsted grade and the local authority** come next. Both are
  random effects in the expectation, and both are questioned below.
- **Disadvantage** matters less than might be expected for all pupils,
  because prior attainment carries much of the same information.
- **The low end.** Segregation adds nothing (AIC
  `r sprintf("%+.1f", imp(A, "Segregation (LA)")$delta_aic)`): it is
  measured at authority level, and the authority's own random effect
  already captures it. Leadership pay and sickness days each move fewer
  than one school in
  `r round(1 / max(imp(A, "Teachers on leadership pay")$moved_quintile, imp(A, "Teacher sickness days")$moved_quintile))`
  a quintile. Teacher retention is the only workforce term that matters
  at all, moving `r pc(imp(A, "Teacher retention")$moved_quintile)` of
  schools. For disadvantaged pupils none of the three workforce terms
  matters (retention's AIC change is
  `r sprintf("%+.1f", imp(D, "Teacher retention")$delta_aic)`).

# What the measure leaves out {#sec-omissions}

If value added correlates with something outside a school's control,
schools are being credited or penalised for it. The published value
added was correlated with each candidate the model leaves out.

```{r fig-omissions}
#| fig-cap: "Correlation across schools between published value added (mean 2021/22 to 2024/25) and variables the model does not include. Teacher retention, disadvantage and prior attainment are in the model and shown for reference; their correlations are near zero by construction."
#| fig-height: 5.2
bind_rows(A$omissions |> mutate(group = "All pupils"),
          D$omissions |> mutate(group = "Disadvantaged pupils")) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, A$omissions$label[order(A$omissions$r)]),
         kind = ifelse(in_model, "In the model", "Left out")) |>
  ggplot(aes(r, label, fill = group, alpha = kind)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`All pupils` = TEAL, `Disadvantaged pupils` = WARM), name = NULL) +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`Left out` = 1, `In the model` = 0.35), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Correlation with value added", y = NULL,
       title = "Value added tracks girls' schools, pupil mobility and neighbourhood education") +
  theme_note(10)
```

Three omissions stand out:

- **Girls' schools** have higher value added (r =
  `r r2(om(A, "girls"))` for all pupils, `r r2(om(D, "girls"))` for
  disadvantaged). Girls outperform boys at GCSE nationally, and the model
  has no term for an intake's gender. Part of what reads as a girls'
  school's added value is its intake.
- **Pupil mobility**, the share of pupils who joined the school during
  the key stage, correlates `r r2(om(A, "mobile"))` with value added.
  Schools that take mid-phase arrivals are penalised for an intake they
  did not choose.
- **Neighbourhood education** correlates `r r2(om(A, "l4"))` for all
  pupils and `r r2(om(D, "l4"))` for disadvantaged pupils. Schools in
  educated places gain a little credit for where they are, and only for
  their non-disadvantaged pupils.

SEN rates, size, governance and religious character are close to
uncorrelated with value added.

# The alternatives {#sec-variants}

Each variant was fitted on the same school-years and compared with the
published value added school by school.

```{r fig-variants}
#| fig-cap: "Each variant against the published model. Across, the change in fit (AIC; left of zero fits better). Up, the share of schools whose value added moves into a different quintile. Removals in red, additions in teal, the combined candidate in purple."
#| fig-height: 6.5
bind_rows(A$variants$summary |> mutate(group = "All pupils"),
          D$variants$summary |> mutate(group = "Disadvantaged pupils")) |>
  filter(spec != "published") |>
  mutate(kind = case_when(spec == "candidate" ~ "Candidate",
                          startsWith(spec, "plus") ~ "Addition", TRUE ~ "Removal"),
         lab = SPEC_LAB[spec]) |>
  ggplot(aes(delta_aic, 100 * moved_quintile, colour = kind)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = lab), size = 2.8, max.overlaps = 30, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~group) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Removal = BAD, Addition = TEAL, Candidate = PURPLE), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Change in AIC against the published model", y = "Schools changing quintile (%)",
       title = "Removing Ofsted or absence moves schools most; mobility and gender are the best additions") +
  theme_note(10)
```

```{r tbl-variants}
#| tbl-cap: "Every variant, all pupils. Fit (AIC change, marginal R²), the local authority variation left (SD of the LA effect, log scale) and Brighton and Hove's rank, and how far school value added moves from the published measure."
A$variants$summary |>
  transmute(Variant = what, `AIC change` = round(delta_aic), `Marginal R²` = sprintf("%.3f", r2_marginal),
            `LA SD` = sprintf("%.4f", sd_la), `B&H rank` = paste(ord(bh_rank), "of", n_la),
            `VA correlation` = sprintf("%.3f", r),
            `Mean change (points)` = sprintf("%.2f", mean_abs_change),
            `Changing quintile` = pc(moved_quintile),
            `Bottom decile kept` = pc(bottom_decile_kept)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrrrrrr")
```

```{r tbl-variants-dis}
#| tbl-cap: "The same for disadvantaged pupils."
D$variants$summary |>
  transmute(Variant = what, `AIC change` = round(delta_aic), `LA SD` = sprintf("%.4f", sd_la),
            `B&H rank` = paste(ord(bh_rank), "of", n_la), `VA correlation` = sprintf("%.3f", r),
            `Mean change (points)` = sprintf("%.2f", mean_abs_change),
            `Changing quintile` = pc(moved_quintile)) |>
  kt(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

A lower AIC is not the test here. Taking out a term the model uses
always worsens the fit. The question for each term is whether it belongs
in the *expectation* a school is measured against.

## Things schools partly control: workforce and Ofsted

**The workforce terms.** Retention, leadership pay and sickness absence
are shaped by a school's leadership as well as by its circumstances. In
the baseline, a school that keeps its teachers is expected to do better,
so the credit for doing so is netted off its value added. Dropping all
three moves `r pc(vs(A, "no_workforce")$moved_quintile)` of schools a
quintile for all pupils, nearly all of it retention, and
`r pc(vs(D, "no_workforce")$moved_quintile)` for disadvantaged pupils.
The fit loss is small (AIC
`r round(vs(A, "no_workforce")$delta_aic)`).

**The Ofsted grade.** This is the more serious problem. Ofsted's
judgements draw on a school's results, so putting the grade in the
expectation partly conditions value added on its own outcome. An
Outstanding school's bar is raised (the grade's random effect has a
standard deviation of
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", imp(A, "Ofsted rating (random)")$std_effect_pct)`),
and some of its added value disappears into it. Removing the grade:

- moves `r pc(vs(A, "no_ofsted")$moved_quintile)` of schools a quintile
  (`r pc(vs(D, "no_ofsted")$moved_quintile)` for disadvantaged pupils);
- changes value added by `r sprintf("%.1f", vs(A, "no_ofsted")$mean_abs_change)`
  points on average, and by more than
  `r sprintf("%.1f", vs(A, "no_ofsted")$p90_abs_change)` for one school
  in ten;
- raises the fixed effects' share of variance (marginal R² from
  `r sprintf("%.2f", vs(A, "published")$r2_marginal)` to
  `r sprintf("%.2f", vs(A, "no_ofsted")$r2_marginal)`), because the
  intake terms take back what the grade had absorbed.

The grade was useful for the Lever report's purpose, which was to
explain attainment. It is the wrong thing to hold constant when the aim
is to measure a school against its intake.

## Intake the model misses: mobility, gender, SEN

- **Mobility** is the best single addition: AIC
  `r round(vs(A, "plus_mobility")$delta_aic)` for all pupils and
  `r round(vs(D, "plus_mobility")$delta_aic)` for disadvantaged. Each
  extra percentage point of mobile pupils costs
  `r sprintf("%.1f%%", abs(pct(cf(A, "plus_mobility", "mobile")$estimate)))` of Attainment 8.
  It moves `r pc(vs(A, "plus_mobility")$moved_quintile)` of schools.
- **Gender.** A girls' school scores
  `r pe(cf(A, "plus_single_sex", "single_sexGirls")$estimate)` above an
  otherwise identical mixed school (boys' schools do not differ, at
  `r pe(cf(A, "plus_single_sex", "single_sexBoys")$estimate)`). A
  single-sex flag (AIC `r round(vs(A, "plus_single_sex")$delta_aic)`)
  fits `r ifelse(vs(A, "plus_single_sex")$delta_aic < vs(A, "plus_girls_pct")$delta_aic, "better", "less well")`
  than the share of girls as a continuous term (AIC
  `r round(vs(A, "plus_girls_pct")$delta_aic)`): the effect is a
  girls'-school effect, not a gradient across mixed schools.
- **SEN.** SEN support and EHCP rates improve the fit modestly for all
  pupils (AIC `r round(vs(A, "plus_sen")$delta_aic)`) and more clearly
  for disadvantaged pupils (`r round(vs(D, "plus_sen")$delta_aic)`), and
  move few schools. They belong in the expectation on principle: a
  school's SEN intake is not of its making.

## Neighbourhood education {#sec-l4}

The preliminary work (Analysis F in the model experiments) found that
the share of adults with degree-level qualifications in the 150 census
output areas nearest a school, about a 2.5 km radius, improved the
model and explained part of the local authority effect. In this
review's terms:

- **For all pupils** it is a strong addition: AIC
  `r round(vs(A, "plus_l4")$delta_aic)`, and one standard deviation of
  neighbourhood education is worth
  `r pe(cf(A, "plus_l4", "z_l4")$estimate)`. The local authority
  standard deviation falls from `r sprintf("%.4f", vs(A, "published")$sd_la)`
  to `r sprintf("%.4f", vs(A, "plus_l4")$sd_la)`: it accounts for
  `r pc(la_var(A, "plus_l4"))` of the authority variance. Brighton and Hove's effect falls from
  `r pe(vs(A, "published")$bh_eff)` (`r ord(vs(A, "published")$bh_rank)`)
  to `r pe(vs(A, "plus_l4")$bh_eff)` (`r ord(vs(A, "plus_l4")$bh_rank)`).
  Part of what looked like a Brighton and Hove effect is the city's
  educated neighbourhoods.
- **For disadvantaged pupils** it does nothing (AIC
  `r sprintf("%+.1f", vs(D, "plus_l4")$delta_aic)`, effect
  `r pe(cf(D, "plus_l4", "z_l4")$estimate)`). Brighton and Hove's rank
  barely moves, from `r ord(vs(D, "published")$bh_rank)` to
  `r ord(vs(D, "plus_l4")$bh_rank)`. Living near educated households does
  not raise disadvantaged pupils' results; it is non-disadvantaged
  pupils, many of whose parents are those households, who carry the
  effect.

That pattern is what one would expect if neighbourhood education stands
in for **parental education**, which no school-level source measures
directly. On that reading it is intake, and belongs in the expectation.
Two cautions:

- it describes the area around the school, not where its pupils live, so
  schools with wide or unusual catchments are measured imperfectly;
- it is fixed at the 2021 Census, so it cannot track change.

## Who runs the school: route and trusts

Converter academies score `r pe(cf(A, "plus_route", "routeConverter academy")$estimate)`
against maintained schools, free schools, UTCs and studio schools
`r pe(cf(A, "plus_route", "routeFree school, UTC or studio")$estimate)`,
and sponsor-led academies
`r pe(cf(A, "plus_route", "routeSponsor-led academy")$estimate)`.
Schools in a multi-academy trust score
`r pe(cf(A, "plus_mat", "in_mat")$estimate)`. None of this moves value
added much (correlations `r r2(vs(A, "plus_route")$r)` and
`r r2(vs(A, "plus_mat")$r)`).

More importantly, **governance should not be in the expectation at all**.
Who runs a school is one of the things value added is meant to reveal:
a trust that improves its schools should see that in their value added,
not have it netted off. The worry about selection, that trusts take on
schools in difficult circumstances, is met by measuring those
circumstances directly (disadvantage, prior attainment, mobility, SEN),
not by adjusting for governance. The trust analysis in the
[East Sussex document](east_sussex.html#sec-trusts) is the right place
for the governance question.

```{r tbl-route}
#| tbl-cap: "Mean value added by governance route (each school's most common route over the four years), under the published model, without workforce and Ofsted, and under the candidate. Attainment 8 points."
bind_rows(A$route_va |> mutate(group = "All pupils"), D$route_va |> mutate(group = "Disadvantaged")) |>
  mutate(spec = SPEC_LAB[spec], va = sprintf("%+.2f", va)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = spec, values_from = va) |>
  select(Group = group, Route = route, Schools = schools, all_of(unname(SPEC_LAB[c("published", "intake_context", "candidate")]))) |>
  kt(align = "llrrrr")
```

## Size and religious character

School size improves the fit for all pupils (AIC
`r round(vs(A, "plus_size")$delta_aic)`) but should stay out: popular,
successful schools grow, so size is partly a consequence of value added.
Religious character makes no difference (AIC
`r sprintf("%+.1f", vs(A, "plus_religious")$delta_aic)`).

## Absence

Absence is the model's second most important term. Dropping it moves
`r pc(vs(A, "no_absence")$moved_quintile)` of schools a quintile, and
Brighton and Hove's authority effect from `r ord(vs(A, "published")$bh_rank)`
in England to `r ord(vs(A, "no_absence")$bh_rank)`. It is partly intake (illness, deprivation) and partly practice.
The Lever report's argument rests on keeping it in, and the joint-signal
plane already shows the other view, value added with attendance counted
in. That pairing is the right answer and needs no change: keep absence
in the core measure, and keep publishing the attendance-counted-in
version beside it.

# Two design choices {#sec-design}

## Against the authority, or against England {#sec-national}

The published value added includes the local authority's random effect
in the expectation. With ten or twenty schools in an authority, that
effect is largely the average of those schools' own results, so part of
each school's added value is attributed to its authority and netted off.
Measuring against England instead (leaving the authority and region
effects out of the prediction):

- correlates `r r2(wn(A)$r[1])` with the published value added across
  schools, and moves `r pc(wn(A)$moved_quintile[1])` of schools a
  quintile (`r pc(wn(D)$moved_quintile[1])` for disadvantaged pupils);
- shifts every school in an authority by the same amount, so it changes
  comparisons *between* authorities, not within them.

```{r fig-national}
#| fig-cap: "Each school's published value added (within its local authority) against its value added measured against England, all pupils, mean 2021/22 to 2024/25. Sussex schools coloured by authority."
#| fig-height: 6
s <- A$design$schools |>
  mutate(area = ifelse(LANAME %in% c("Brighton and Hove", "East Sussex", "West Sussex"), LANAME, "Rest of England"))
ggplot(s, aes(pub_la, pub_nat)) +
  geom_abline(colour = GREY, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = filter(s, area == "Rest of England"), colour = LIGHT, size = 0.7, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = filter(s, area != "Rest of England"), aes(fill = area), shape = 21,
             colour = "white", size = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = AREA_COL, name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = quantile(s$pub_la, c(0.002, 0.998)), ylim = quantile(s$pub_nat, c(0.002, 0.998))) +
  labs(x = "Published value added, within the local authority (points)",
       y = "Value added against England (points)",
       title = "Brighton and Hove's schools sit above the line: their authority effect is netted off") +
  theme_note(10)
```

Both views are legitimate, but they answer different questions:

- **Within the authority:** "how does this school do compared with
  similar schools *in the same place*?"
- **Against England:** "how does this school do compared with similar
  schools anywhere?"

For the Sussex documents, which compare schools across three
authorities, the national version is the right one, and the authority
effect should be reported beside it rather than inside it.

## How much of value added is the school {#sec-signal}

A version of the published model with a school random intercept splits
the unexplained variation into a persistent school part and year-to-year
noise:

- **All pupils:** the school part has a standard deviation of
  `r sprintf("%.3f", A$design$school_sd)` (log scale) against
  `r sprintf("%.3f", A$design$resid_sd)` for the year-to-year noise.
  `r pc(A$design$icc)` of the unexplained variation is persistent. A
  four-year average has a reliability of
  `r r2(A$design$reliability_mean)`.
- **Disadvantaged pupils:** `r pc(D$design$icc)` persistent, and a
  four-year average reliability of `r r2(D$design$reliability_mean)`.
  The groups are small, and single years are noisy.

The shrunken school effects from that model correlate
`r r2(A$design$blup_vs_mean)` with the averaged residuals for all
pupils, and `r r2(D$design$blup_vs_mean)` for disadvantaged pupils. The
simple average is a good approximation. The shrunken estimate is better
for small schools and should be preferred where single schools are
singled out.

# What it would mean in Sussex

```{r tbl-sussex}
#| tbl-cap: "Value added for each Sussex school, all pupils, mean 2021/22 to 2024/25, Attainment 8 points: as published (within its local authority), against England, and under the candidate measure against England. Ordered by authority and published value added."
A$sussex |>
  arrange(LANAME, desc(pub_la)) |>
  transmute(School = SCHNAME, Authority = LANAME,
            Published = sprintf("%+.1f", pub_la), `Against England` = sprintf("%+.1f", pub_nat),
            `Candidate, against England` = sprintf("%+.1f", cand_nat),
            Change = sprintf("%+.1f", cand_nat - pub_la)) |>
  kt(align = "llrrrr")
```

```{r sussex-notes}
#| include: false
sx <- A$sussex |> group_by(LANAME) |>
  summarise(shift_nat = mean(pub_nat - pub_la), shift_cand = mean(cand_nat - pub_la), .groups = "drop")
sh <- function(la, col) sx[[col]][sx$LANAME == la]
```

Measured against England, Brighton and Hove's schools gain
`r sprintf("%+.1f", sh("Brighton and Hove", "shift_nat"))` points on
average, East Sussex's `r sprintf("%+.1f", sh("East Sussex", "shift_nat"))`
and West Sussex's `r sprintf("%+.1f", sh("West Sussex", "shift_nat"))`:
the published measure nets each authority's effect off its own schools.
Under the candidate measure against England the average changes are
`r sprintf("%+.1f", sh("Brighton and Hove", "shift_cand"))`,
`r sprintf("%+.1f", sh("East Sussex", "shift_cand"))` and
`r sprintf("%+.1f", sh("West Sussex", "shift_cand"))`. The Sussex
documents' comparisons across authorities would change in that
direction.

# Recommendations {#sec-recommendations}

1. **Keep the construction.** A school-level residual of a multilevel
   model of log Attainment 8, by pupil group, is the right measure. Keep
   prior attainment, absence, disadvantage, EAL and selective admissions
   at its core.
2. **Take the Ofsted rating out of the value-added model.** It
   conditions value added on a judgement made partly from the same
   results. This is the most consequential change. Ofsted can stay in
   explanatory models (and the area decompositions) where the aim is to
   describe attainment rather than to measure schools.
3. **Take the workforce terms out of the value-added model.** Leadership
   pay and sickness add almost nothing. Retention adds a little, but it
   is partly an outcome of how a school is led. All three are better used
   to *explain* value added than to set its baseline.
4. **Drop LA segregation.** It adds nothing once the authority's own
   effect is in the model.
5. **Add pupil mobility, a girls' school term, and SEN support and EHCP
   rates.** All are intake, all improve the fit, and mobility and gender
   remove clear biases in the current measure. A single-sex flag fits
   better than the share of girls.
6. **Add neighbourhood education for all-pupil and non-disadvantaged
   value added.** It stands in for parental education, removes the
   current tilt towards schools in educated places, and accounts for
   `r pc(la_var(A, "plus_l4"))` of the local authority variance. Including it for
   disadvantaged pupils is harmless but makes no difference, so the
   specification can be shared across the three groups for simplicity.
7. **Leave governance, size and religious character out.** Who runs a
   school is something value added should reveal, not absorb. Size is
   partly a consequence of success.
8. **Report value added against England as well as within the
   authority**, and use the national version wherever schools in
   different authorities are compared. Report the authority effect
   separately.
9. **Keep absence in, and keep publishing the attendance-counted-in
   view beside it**, as the joint-signal plane already does.
10. **Use shrunken school effects, with intervals, where single schools
    are named**, especially for disadvantaged pupils, whose four-year
    reliability is `r r2(D$design$reliability_mean)`.

Recommendations 2, 3, 5 and 6 together are the "candidate" measured in
this review (it keeps segregation, which makes no difference either
way). Recommendation 8 is a reporting choice and can be applied to
either model.

**Effect on the published work.** The Lever report's argument rests on
the model's explanatory terms, chiefly absence, and the candidate leaves
those intact. What would change is the ranking of individual schools and
the comparisons between authorities. If adopted, the change should be
introduced as a new, labelled measure alongside the published one,
not as a silent revision. The Sussex documents would move to it, with a
note.

# Notes on method {.unnumbered}

All models are fitted to the published model's own data
(`data/model_data_imputed.rds`): 2021/22 to 2024/25, with 2024/25's
workforce and prior-attainment terms carried forward as in the published
model. The common sample drops the
`r format(12210 - R$n, big.mark = ",")` school-years with no
neighbourhood or mobility figure. Value added is computed exactly as
published (bias-corrected back-transformation, every random effect in
the prediction) unless stated. AIC comparisons use maximum likelihood;
value added uses REML fits. Neighbourhood education is the share of
adults with level 4+ qualifications in the 150 nearest 2021 Census
output areas (`R/13_census_context.R`). Mobility is 100 minus the share
of pupils who were at the school throughout the key stage. Trust
membership is by year, from the DfE exclusions file
(`R/19_trust_effects.R`). The analysis is `R/21_value_added_review.R`;
this document is `value_added_review.qmd`.
